hook.text: You remember a picture of a sunset better than the word "sunset." Images stick harder than words.

buildup.text: Allan Paivio's dual coding theory says memory has two channels: one verbal, one visual.

discovery.text: When information is encoded in both channels, you get two retrieval routes instead of one.

twist.text: Concrete words like "dog" are easier to visualize than abstract words like "justice"—and better recalled.

climax.text: This is why diagrams plus text outperform text alone. Two codes are always better than one.

punchline.text: See it and say it. Remember it twice.

quiz.question: What does dual coding theory propose about memory?
options: Two channels—verbal and visual—create stronger memories

details.summary: Paivio's dual coding theory states that information encoded in both verbal and visual forms is remembered better than information encoded in only one form. Words paired with images create two independent memory traces, doubling retrieval pathways.
details.whyItMatters: Dual coding provides a simple principle for instructional design: combine words with visuals. It doubles the routes to retrieval and produces more robust memory.
takeaways: Verbal plus visual encoding creates two memory pathways
Redundant coding provides backup retrieval routes
Diagrams and images consistently enhance text-based learning

faq.question: Does dual coding mean everyone is a visual learner?
faq.answer: No. Dual coding benefits everyone, not just visual learners. The learning styles myth has been debunked by research. The advantage comes from having two codes rather than one, not from matching a preferred style. Everyone benefits from combining words and meaningful images.

faq.question: What kinds of visuals work best for dual coding?
faq.answer: Visuals that add meaning to the text are best: diagrams, concept maps, timelines, and annotated illustrations. Decorative images that do not relate to the content do not help and can distract. The visual must be integrated with the verbal information, not merely placed alongside it.
